GitHub Issue:
Post Date: 2021-06-08T16:17:32Z
Current Date: April 4 2025
Title: Methos to() requires mock in unit test
Description: Hi. could you please clarify question?
I Have the following method
```
public Single<Book> load(String bookName, String author) {
        return bookRepo.load(bookName)
                .switchIfEmpty(Observable.error(EntityNotFoundException::new))
                .toList()
                .flatMap(books-> bookService.loadbookByAuthor(Observable.fromIterable(books), autor)
                        .switchIfEmpty(Maybe.error(() -> new ValidationErrorException()))
                        .toSingle());
    }
```

And I have unit test for this method. which works
```
public void shouldValidatePolicyExists() {
        when(bookRepo.load(any())).thenReturn(Observable.empty());

        testObject.load(request).test()
                .assertError(EntityNotFoundException.class)
    }
```

I want to get rid of toList() in my method and found the following way
```
public Single<Book> load(String bookName, String author) {
        return bookRepo.load(bookName)
                .switchIfEmpty(Observable.error(EntityNotFoundException::new))
                .to(books-> bookService.loadbookByAuthor(books, autor)
                        .switchIfEmpty(Maybe.error(() -> new ValidationErrorException()))
                        .toSingle());
    }
```
But unit test does not work for this method implementation.
It does not return EntityNotFoundException and requires bookService is mocked.
Could you please clarify why ?

REASONING: This issue is about understanding why a unit test fails after refactoring RxJava code from using `toList().flatMap()` to using the `to()` operator. This is a conceptual issue related to RxJava behavior that can be analyzed without building or running the code. The problem is that the `to()` operator works differently than `toList().flatMap()` - it's a higher-order function that changes how the stream is processed, affecting when and how the mocks are called. The issue can be verified by analyzing the RxJava documentation and understanding the difference in behavior between these operators. A knowledgeable developer can explain why the test fails without needing to compile or run the code, as it's about understanding RxJava operator semantics rather than an issue that requires actual execution to diagnose.
